pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** How Materials Change State

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry & Physics 'Matter'):** Changes of state in terms of the particle model; conservation of material and of mass, and reversibility, in melting, freezing, evaporation, sublimation, condensation; changes with temperature in motion and spacing of particles; internal energy stored in materials.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-4):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-4].

- **Operational details:** This node explains ALL the state changes — melting, freezing, boiling, condensing, sublimation — at the particle level, and reads HEATING/COOLING CURVES. Core ideas: adding thermal energy makes particles move faster and (at a transition) overcome the forces holding them, changing state; the reverse on cooling. The subtle, high-value idea is the PLATEAU: during a change of state the temperature stays CONSTANT even though heating continues, because the energy goes into breaking particle bonds (changing arrangement), not raising kinetic energy — the flat regions of the curve mark the melting and boiling points. Also distinguish evaporation (surface, any temperature) from boiling (throughout the liquid, at the boiling point). Link back to the particle model (prereq) and conservation (same particles throughout). Keep energy qualitative (no latent-heat calculations).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early-formal). The child names each state change, describes the particle behaviour for it, reads a heating curve to identify melting/boiling points from the flat regions, and explains WHY temperature holds constant during a change of state.
bestPractices: Link three views — heating control, particle behaviour, and the temperature-vs-time graph — so the curve's shape is tied to what particles are doing.
Make the plateau the centrepiece: energy during a change of state breaks particle bonds rather than raising temperature.
Distinguish evaporation (surface, any temperature) from boiling (throughout, at the boiling point) explicitly.
Cover the full set including sublimation, and show cooling as the mirror image.
Keep energy qualitative (no latent-heat calculations) and reinforce that the same particles persist (conservation).
keyRepresentations: A synchronised burner / particle-beaker / heating-curve triple view
A heating and cooling curve with flat regions at melting and boiling points
Particle snapshots for each state change (melt, freeze, boil, condense, sublime)
commonMisconceptions: Temperature keeps rising during melting/boiling even though heat is still added (missing the latent-heat plateau).
Evaporation and boiling are the same thing.
Boiling bubbles are air or oxygen rather than the substance's own vapour.
Freezing 'adds cold' rather than removing energy.
Particles are created or destroyed, or change size, during a state change (rather than only rearranging and changing speed).

learn.summary: For ages 11–12: explain the main changes of state (melting, freezing, boiling, condensing, sublimation) using the particle model, and read heating/cooling curves to find melting and boiling points from their flat regions. The high-value idea is the plateau: for a pure substance, during a change of state the temperature stays constant even while heating continues, because incoming energy overcomes the forces holding particles in their arrangement rather than increasing particle speed (mixtures such as wax or chocolate tend to melt over a range of temperatures instead). Learners also distinguish evaporation (from the surface, at any temperature) from boiling (throughout the liquid, at the boiling point), and see cooling as the mirror image with the same particles throughout (conservation). Keep energy qualitative — no latent-heat calculations.

activities.title: Change-of-state studio: link heating, particles, and the curve
feedback: If a learner expects the thermometer to keep rising during melting, pause on the plateau and show that the incoming energy is overcoming the forces holding particles in their arrangement (rearranging them, letting them move past one another), so temperature holds until the change is complete, then climbs again.

If a learner reads the flat region but not its cause, prompt: during the flat part the particles are breaking free/rearranging; during the sloping part the particles are speeding up (temperature rising).
If a learner treats evaporation and boiling as identical, replay both modes: evaporation happens at the surface at any temperature; boiling happens throughout at the boiling point.
Reinforce that no particles are created, destroyed, or resized — they only rearrange and change speed; this is why mass is conserved and the change is reversible.
activities.rationale: Tying the curve's shape to what particles are doing under a controllable heat input is intended to make the plateau's meaning observable rather than asserted; a self-tracing graph linked to live particle behaviour aims to make the relationship between heating, particle arrangement, and temperature concrete. This is a research-informed design proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3: changes of state in terms of the particle model; conservation and reversibility in melting/freezing/evaporation/sublimation/condensation; changes with temperature in motion and spacing of particles; internal energy
NGSS MS-PS1-4: model predicting/describing changes in particle motion, temperature and state as thermal energy is added/removed
Students expect temperature to keep rising through a change of state (missing the latent-heat plateau) and conflate evaporation with boiling
learnerActions: Use a heat/cool control and watch three linked panels together: a heat source, a beaker of particles, and a temperature-vs-time graph that draws itself as time passes.
Crank up the heat on a solid and observe the particles vibrate harder, then at the melting point break loose and move past one another as a liquid — and note that exactly there the graph goes flat.
Keep the heat full on during the flat region and read the thermometer: notice it refuses to climb during melting even though heating continues.
Continue heating to the boiling plateau, then run a cooling trace and watch the mirror-image curve form while tracking that the same particles persist throughout.
Toggle between a surface-evaporation mode (slow, at any temperature) and a boiling mode (bubbles of the substance's own vapour forming throughout the liquid at the boiling point) and compare.
Explore sublimation as a direct solid-to-gas change.
activities.intendedInsight: During a change of state the temperature holds constant because energy goes into rearranging particles (overcoming the forces holding them in their arrangement) rather than increasing their speed; the flat regions of the curve mark the melting and boiling points. Evaporation and boiling differ (surface/any temperature vs throughout/at the boiling point), and the same particles persist throughout.

activities.title: Predict-Observe-Explain: heating crushed ice
feedback: If the prediction is a straight rising line ('you're still heating it, so it gets hotter'), plot the real curve with its plateau and explain the energy is spent rearranging particles during the change; read the flat region as the melting point.
Full understanding needs the reason — 'energy goes into the state change, not into heating' — not just reading the plateau.
For the washing-line puzzle: evaporation happens from the surface at any temperature, so water leaves slowly even in the cold; it does not require reaching 100°C.
For freezing: expect a flat part at the freezing point (0°C for water) as energy is removed and particles lock into the solid arrangement — the mirror image of melting.
activities.rationale: Asking for a before-observation prediction and its reason is diagnostic: the plateau is counter-intuitive, so a naive 'heat in means temperature up' model predicts a steady rise. The reason, not the reading, reveals whether the mechanism is understood. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Students expect temperature to keep rising through a change of state (missing the latent-heat plateau) and conflate evaporation with boiling
learnerActions: Before doing anything, predict the temperature-vs-time graph for a thermometer in crushed ice that is heated steadily — especially what happens while ice and water coexist — and write WHY you predict that shape.
Heat crushed ice (taken to start at 0°C) steadily, stirring gently, with a thermometer in it and record the temperature over time, plotting the trace.

Compare your prediction with your real trace, which should show an approximately flat region at or near 0°C while ice and water coexist (a well-stirred mixture stays close to 0°C; small rises can happen if water near the heat source warms before all the ice has melted).
Explain where the heat energy 'goes' during the flat part, and answer: would freezing water show a flat part too, and at what temperature and why?
Apply the idea to a puzzle: wet clothes dry on a cold washing line — how, if water only turns to gas at 100°C?
activities.intendedInsight: The thermometer stays at about 0°C while ice and water coexist in a well-stirred mixture because the incoming energy overcomes the forces/arrangement holding the solid particles (changing state) rather than raising particle speed; only once all the ice has melted does the temperature rise clearly again. Evaporation from a surface occurs at any temperature, which is why cold wet clothes dry.

activities.title: Annotated heating/cooling curve reference
feedback: Prompt the learner to say, for any point on the curve, whether particles are speeding up (sloping region) or breaking free/rearranging (flat region).
Check that melting and boiling points are read from the flat regions, not from the peaks or endpoints.
activities.rationale: A labelled, reveal-based curve is a strong canonical reference for graph-reading and consolidation. As a fixed reference it supports reading and recall; it does not let the learner drive heating and watch the curve and particles change in real time, so it complements rather than replaces a dynamic activity.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3: changes of state in terms of the particle model; conservation and reversibility in melting/freezing/evaporation/sublimation/condensation; changes with temperature in motion and spacing of particles; internal energy
learnerActions: Study a labelled heating and cooling curve with the flat regions marked as the melting and boiling points.
Reveal 'why temperature is constant' explanations attached to each flat region, and match each segment to a paired particle snapshot (solid vibrating, melting, liquid, boiling, gas).
Use this as a paper/reference consolidation after the studio activity: practise reading melting and boiling points off a curve and stating what particles are doing in each region.
activities.intendedInsight: A heating or cooling curve can be read for melting and boiling points at its flat regions, with each region corresponding to a specific particle behaviour and a reason for constant temperature during a change of state.

activities.title: Check: name, describe, read, and explain state changes
feedback: For curve-reading errors, point back to the flat regions as the transition temperatures.
If matching or sequencing is wrong, revisit the particle snapshots to reconnect each change to its particle behaviour.
Where the explanation of constant temperature is missing or mechanical, prompt for 'energy into overcoming the particle arrangement, not into particle speed'.
activities.rationale: Curve-reading, matching particle descriptions, and sequencing are apt ways to probe this node; pairing after the dynamic activity lets the learner apply what they observed. A recognition/matching check confirms reading and classification but does not by itself elicit independent construction of the explanation, so an open explanation prompt is included.
sourceClaims: NGSS MS-PS1-4: model predicting/describing changes in particle motion, temperature and state as thermal energy is added/removed
learnerActions: Read a heating curve and identify the melting point and boiling point from the flat regions (e.g. using a slider or by labelling).
Match each state change (melt, freeze, boil, condense, sublime) to its correct particle-level description.
Sequence the states a substance passes through as it is heated or cooled.
Explain in your own words why temperature stays constant during a change of state, and distinguish evaporation from boiling.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates naming each change of state, describing the particle behaviour, reading melting/boiling points from a curve, and explaining the plateau mechanism and the evaporation/boiling distinction.

constraints: Keep energy qualitative: no latent-heat calculations at this level.
Reinforce conservation: the same particles persist throughout; particles are not created, destroyed, or resized during a state change — they only rearrange and change speed.
Melting and boiling points are read from the flat regions of the curve, not its endpoints or peaks.
The labelled curve reference is a fixed consolidation aid: it supports reading and recall but cannot be driven by the learner to show particles and graph changing in real time.
A recognition/matching assessment confirms classification and graph-reading but does not on its own show the learner can independently construct the plateau explanation; pair it with an open prompt.
Boiling bubbles are the substance's own vapour (gaseous water), not dissolved air, oxygen, or 'heat'.
Freezing removes energy rather than 'adding cold'.
Describe the energy as overcoming the forces/arrangement between particles; at this level 'bonds between particles' is an acceptable simplification for those intermolecular forces.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source marks the misconception/change-of-state research claim (BEST / AAAS Project 2061) as verified:false; treat its evidence strength as unconfirmed.

The source frames a dynamic simulation as 'ideal' and a static curve and dialogue as weaker for this node. These are catalog fit judgements, not established comparative efficacy; the rewrite presents them as a primary dynamic activity plus a complementary reference without claiming any medium is universally necessary. A 3D particle box and an in-role dialogue were noted as lower-fit in the source but can still support aspects of this topic.

No provided source claim directly validates the specific interactive design's effectiveness; the curriculum (DfE/NGSS) claims ground the content taught, and the BEST claim motivates addressing the plateau misconception.
The POE pre-observation prediction-and-reason is the intended diagnostic element; ensure learners commit a prediction before heating.

The POE task takes crushed ice as starting exactly at 0°C (inherited from the source). Real crushed ice may begin below 0°C and show an initial rising segment before the melting plateau; the 0°C start is an idealisation kept from the source.
'Bonds' between particles here means intermolecular forces between molecules, not intramolecular chemical bonds; retained as an age-appropriate simplification inherited from the source.

'Prising particles apart' wording from the source was replaced with 'overcoming the forces holding particles in their arrangement', because solid→liquid melting barely increases particle spacing; the forces-overcoming framing is accurate for both melting and boiling plateaus.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: put a thermometer in crushed ice and heat steadily, asking the child to predict the temperature-vs-time graph BEFORE starting — especially what happens while ice and water coexist — and WHY. A 'heat always raises temperature' model draws a straight rising line. The real trace shows a plateau at 0°C. The pre-observation prediction and its reason are the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: On your heating curve, what is happening to the particles during the FLAT part versus the sloping part?
Where does the heat energy 'go' while the temperature isn't changing?
Wet clothes dry on a cold washing line — how, if water only turns to gas at 100°C?
Freezing water: would you expect a flat part too? At what temperature, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: The thermometer stays STUCK at 0°C while ice and water coexist. The heat energy going in is used to break the bonds/arrangement holding the solid particles — changing state — rather than to raise the temperature (particle speed). Only once all the ice has melted does the temperature start rising again. Full marks need 'energy goes into the state change, not into heating'.

errorPatterns.pattern: temperature must keep rising whenever you add heat ('you're heating it, so it gets hotter')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show/plot the real curve with its plateau; explain energy is spent rearranging particles during the change, so temperature holds. Read the flat region as the melting point.
errorPatterns.distractor: It keeps rising — you're still heating it, so it gets hotter.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: predicts a steadily rising temperature with no flat region during melting

errorPatterns.pattern: evaporation and boiling are the same thing / evaporation only happens at the boiling point
errorPatterns.nextMove: Evaporation happens from the SURFACE at any temperature (wet clothes dry in the cold); boiling happens THROUGHOUT at the boiling point. Contrast the two directly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says a puddle can only dry up if heated to 100°C, or can't distinguish surface evaporation from throughout-boiling

errorPatterns.pattern: the bubbles in boiling water are air, or are 'heat', not water vapour
errorPatterns.nextMove: The bubbles are water that has turned to gas (vapour) inside the liquid — not dissolved air, not heat. Link to condensation reappearing on a cold lid.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: identifies boiling bubbles as air/oxygen rather than gaseous water

responseLevels.gap: Predicts steadily rising temperature through melting; treats added heat as always raising temperature; conflates evaporation with boiling.
responseLevels.full: Explains the plateau as energy going into rearranging particles (state change) not raising temperature, reads melting/boiling points from flat regions, AND distinguishes surface evaporation (any temperature) from throughout-boiling (at boiling point), transferring the idea to freezing.
responseLevels.partial: Identifies the plateau and reads melting/boiling points off a curve, but can't explain WHY temperature holds (energy into the state change) or distinguish evaporation from boiling — reads the graph without the mechanism.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I keep a thermometer in a beaker of crushed ice and heat it steadily. The ice starts at 0°C. While the ice is still melting — some ice, some water in the beaker — what does the thermometer read: rising, falling, or stuck? Then the key part: explain WHY the temperature does that while ice and water are both present.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason separates a child who understands the plateau (energy diverted to the change of state) from one who assumes 'heat in always means temperature up'. The plateau is counter-intuitive, so a naive model predicts steady rising — the reason, not the reading, reveals the understanding.
